questions.question: In a normal-form game with players $N$, profile set $S$ and payoff functions $v_i$, when does a profile $s$ Pareto dominate a profile $s'$?
options: Only when $v_i(s)>v_i(s')$ holds strictly for every single player $i\in N$
When the total payoff satisfies $\sum_{i\in N}v_i(s)>\sum_{i\in N}v_i(s')$
When $v_i(s)\ge v_i(s')$ for all $i\in N$ and $v_j(s)>v_j(s')$ for some $j$
When $v_i(s)\ge v_i(s')$ holds for at least one player $i\in N$ of the game

questions.question: In a finite two-player game, profile $s$ gives player 1 a payoff of $10$ and player 2 a payoff of $0$, and every other profile gives player 1 strictly less than $10$. What can be said about $s$?
options: It is not efficient, because player 2 receives nothing in it.
It is Pareto efficient, however unequal its payoffs are.
It is efficient only if player 2 would agree to it being played.
It cannot be judged without first fixing a fair split of payoffs.

questions.question: In some normal-form game, profile $s$ is Pareto efficient and profile $s'$ is not. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Some profile Pareto dominates $s'$, though it need not be $s$.
Every player gets at least as much in $s$ as in $s'$.
The profile $s$ Pareto dominates the profile $s'$.
The total payoff in $s$ is larger than the total in $s'$.

questions.question: Each player chooses $C$ or $D$, with payoffs $(v_1,v_2)$ given by $(C,C)=(5,5)$, $(C,D)=(0,7)$, $(D,C)=(7,0)$ and $(D,D)=(2,2)$. Which statement about Pareto dominance holds?
options: $(C,D)$ Pareto dominates $(D,D)$, as its total $7$ exceeds $4$.
$(D,C)$ Pareto dominates $(C,C)$, as player 1 gets $7$ instead of $5$.
No profile at all Pareto dominates the profile $(D,D)$ here.
$(C,C)$ Pareto dominates $(D,D)$, and $(C,D)$ does not.

questions.question: Player 1 chooses a row, player 2 a column, and cells list $(v_1,v_2)$: row $T$: $L$: $(4,1)$, $R$: $(2,2)$; row $B$: $L$: $(3,3)$, $R$: $(1,0)$. Which profiles are Pareto efficient?
options: $(B,L)$ only
$(T,L)$ and $(B,L)$ only
$(T,R)$ and $(B,L)$ only

questions.question: Two players each choose $O$ or $F$. Matching on $O$ gives $(3,1)$, matching on $F$ gives $(1,3)$, and each mismatch gives $(0,0)$. Which profiles are Pareto efficient?
options: Only $(O,O)$, since player 1 likes it best
None, since $(O,O)$ and $(F,F)$ cannot be ranked
All four, since no single profile beats all others
$(O,O)$ and $(F,F)$, but neither mismatch

questions.question: Two different strategy profiles $s$ and $s'$ of a two-player game yield exactly the same payoff vector, $(2,2)$. Which statement is correct?
options: Each of the two profiles Pareto dominates the other.
Neither of the two profiles Pareto dominates the other.
Neither can be Pareto efficient, since their payoffs tie.
They count as one profile, as profiles are identified by payoffs.

questions.question: Why does every finite normal-form game have at least one Pareto-efficient profile?
options: In a finite game some profile Pareto dominates every other profile, and that profile is efficient.
Pareto dominance is complete, so on a finite set of profiles it always has a greatest element.
A profile maximising $\sum_i v_i$ exists, and a Pareto improvement on it would raise that sum.
The profile giving each player his own highest payoff exists in any finite game and is efficient.

questions.question: In a normal-form game with profile set $S$, which condition is the defining criterion for a profile $s^*\in S$ to be Pareto efficient?
options: When $s^*$ Pareto dominates every other profile in $S$
When $s^*$ gives each player the same payoff as the others
When $s^*$ maximises the sum of all players' payoffs on $S$
When no profile in $S$ Pareto dominates $s^*$

questions.question: Two firms are the players of a pricing game, and each firm's payoff is its own profit. Changing from profile $s'$ to profile $s$ raises both firms' profits but lowers the consumers' surplus. Judged within the game, which statement is correct?
options: $s$ Pareto dominates $s'$: only the players' payoffs count.
It is no Pareto improvement, because the consumers lose out.
$s$ dominates $s'$ only if the firms' gain exceeds the consumers' loss.
The profiles are incomparable, since the change affects outsiders.

questions.question: View Pareto dominance as a relation on the profile set $S$ of a normal-form game. Which property does this relation fail to have in general?
options: Transitivity: dominance of $s$ over $t$ and of $t$ over $u$ implies dominance of $s$ over $u$.
Irreflexivity: for every feasible profile $s$, Pareto dominance of $s$ over itself is ruled out.
Completeness: for every two distinct profiles $s,t$, either $s$ dominates $t$ or $t$ dominates $s$.
Asymmetry: dominance of $s$ over $t$ rules out dominance of $t$ over $s$ in the reverse direction.

questions.question: At profile $s$ of a normal-form game, no single player can raise his own payoff by changing only his own strategy. What follows about the Pareto efficiency of $s$?
options: $s$ is Pareto efficient, because no player is able to do better.
Nothing: some other profile may still be better for every player.
$s$ is Pareto efficient, provided the game has finitely many profiles.
$s$ is never Pareto efficient, as stable profiles are always dominated.

questions.question: Player 1 chooses a row, player 2 a column: row $T$: $L$: $(5,0)$, $R$: $(1,1)$; row $B$: $L$: $(2,2)$, $R$: $(0,4)$. The total at $(B,L)$ is $4$, below the total $5$ at $(T,L)$. Is $(B,L)$ Pareto efficient?
options: Yes: no profile gives both players at least $2$ and someone more.
No: $(T,L)$ has the larger total, so it Pareto dominates $(B,L)$.
No: only a profile with the largest total can be Pareto efficient.
Yes, and the reason is that $(B,L)$ gives both players equal payoffs.

questions.question: A game has three players. Four of its profiles give the payoff vectors $a=(2,2,2)$, $b=(3,2,2)$, $c=(4,1,5)$ and $d=(2,3,1)$. Which of $b$, $c$, $d$ Pareto dominate $a$?
options: $b$ and $c$
$c$ only
$b$, $c$ and $d$
$b$ only

questions.question: A profile $s$ of a normal-form game is known to be Pareto efficient. Which conclusion about $s$ is justified?
options: None about single deviations: a player may gain by switching alone.
No player can raise his own payoff by changing only his own strategy.
Each player is at least as well off in $s$ as in any other profile.
$s$ gives the largest possible total payoff among all profiles in $S$.

questions.question: In a finite two-player game, profile $s$ gives player 1 the highest payoff he gets in any profile. Which statement is correct?
options: $s$ is always Pareto efficient, as no profile improves on it for player 1.
$s$ is Pareto efficient only when it also maximises player 2's payoff.
$s$ Pareto dominates every profile giving player 1 a lower payoff.
$s$ can be dominated if another profile ties for player 1 and helps player 2.

questions.question: Player 1 chooses a row, player 2 a column: row $T$: $L$: $(3,2)$, $C$: $(3,4)$, $R$: $(1,5)$; row $B$: $L$: $(4,1)$, $C$: $(2,2)$, $R$: $(4,1)$. How many of the six profiles are Pareto efficient?

Player 1 chooses a row, player 2 a column: row $T$: $L$: $(4,1)$, $R$: $(1,1)$; row $B$: $L$: $(2,4)$, $R$: $(0,0)$. Now every payoff of player 1 is multiplied by $3$, player 2's payoffs unchanged. What happens?
options: Both the efficient set and the total-maximising profile stay exactly the same.
The efficient set stays $\{(T,L),(B,L)\}$, but the total-maximising profile changes.
The efficient set shrinks to $\{(T,L)\}$, the profile with the new largest total.
The efficient set changes, because the payoff totals of the profiles change.
